Tokenizer boundary misalignment occurs when a shared multilingual vocabulary segments morphologically similar or semantically equivalent words differently across languages — for instance, the Turkish word kitaplar ("books") might tokenize as a single unit or two subwords depending on vocabulary coverage, while its English equivalent splits cleanly at the morpheme boundary, creating structurally asymmetric representations that the model must somehow align in embedding space. The central question is whether cross-lingual transfer degrades not because of insufficient shared vocabulary or domain mismatch, but because the granularity of subword decomposition varies so much across languages that aligned semantic concepts occupy fundamentally incompatible positions in the representation manifold. Experts worry specifically about fertility mismatch — the ratio of tokens produced per word varying by 3–5× between high- and low-resource languages in a shared vocabulary — because this means low-resource languages consume disproportionate context window budget per semantic unit, diluting the effective signal density during both pretraining and fine-tuning. A beginner sees this as a vocabulary coverage problem solvable by adding more multilingual data; an expert sees it as a geometric problem where the same fine-tuning gradient update simultaneously nudges representations for languages whose subword boundaries carve meaning at completely different joints, creating systematic interference rather than transfer. The deeper worry is that boundary-induced fragmentation in morphologically rich languages (Swahili, Finnish, Turkish) causes the model to learn surface concatenation patterns rather than compositional morpheme semantics, meaning that transfer from English — where root meanings are often lexically atomic — actively distorts the compositional structure the target language relies on.

When a high-fertility language like Turkish or Amharic tokenizes a single semantic unit into 4–6 subword tokens against English's 1–2, the attention mechanism faces a structural asymmetry: each English token must distribute its attention mass across a proportionally larger span of target-side tokens to achieve semantic correspondence, thinning attention weights per token and creating what amounts to a diffuse alignment signal rather than sharp cross-lingual anchoring. Empirically, Chi et al. (2020) in "Finding Fast in Transformers" demonstrated that cross-lingual alignment is not uniformly distributed but concentrates in middle layers (roughly layers 7–16 in a 24-layer mBERT), precisely where token-level representations begin abstracting away from surface form — but fertility mismatch stresses exactly these layers because the positional spread of a single concept differs by language, forcing the model to learn inconsistent span-to-concept mappings. In high-fertility conditions, lower layers spend additional capacity encoding intra-word compositional relationships (prefix, root, suffix boundaries) rather than cross-lingual semantic grounding, effectively pushing the layer at which meaningful alignment becomes possible upward, compressing the alignment-capable window. Wu and Dredze (2020) showed that low-resource, morphologically rich languages in mBERT exhibit weaker cross-lingual transfer precisely in tasks requiring span-level semantic coherence (NER, dependency parsing) compared to token-classification tasks, consistent with fertility-induced attention diffusion degrading span representations specifically. The practical implication is that cross-lingual alignment probes — like those used in Libovický et al. (2020) on mBERT — find strongest alignment signal in middle layers for balanced-fertility language pairs, but this signal migrates toward upper layers and weakens in magnitude for high-fertility targets, meaning that fine-tuning protocols that freeze lower layers (a common parameter-efficient strategy) inadvertently freeze the very compositional machinery the high-fertility language needs to restructure.

Fine-tuning on a high-resource pivot like English does demonstrably overwrite upper-layer cross-lingual alignment: Merchant et al. (2020) showed that task-specific fine-tuning causes the upper layers of mBERT to rapidly specialize toward the fine-tuning language's surface statistics, with representational similarity (measured via CKA) between source and target languages dropping most sharply in layers 9–12 after as few as 1000 gradient steps — precisely the layers where morphologically rich language alignment was already compressed. This catastrophic interference is asymmetric: English representations remain stable because their alignment was never dependent on upper layers to begin with, while Turkish or Swahili representations, having no lower-layer fallback, lose their cross-lingual grounding almost entirely. The most principled architectural intervention is language-specific adapter layers inserted at upper transformer blocks, as in MAD-X (Pfeiffer et al., 2020), which freezes the shared backbone and trains separate adapter modules per language — this surgically prevents pivot fine-tuning from modifying the parameters carrying cross-lingual alignment for low-resource languages, with reported gains of 10–20 F1 points on NER for high-fertility African and Southeast Asian languages. A complementary training intervention is cross-lingual consistency regularization, where an auxiliary loss penalizes divergence between the upper-layer representations of semantically equivalent source and target sentences during fine-tuning, forcing the model to preserve alignment geometry even as task-specific information accumulates — Cao et al. (2020) applied a variant of this using parallel sentences as anchors and recovered substantial transfer on XNLI for morphologically rich languages. The deeper architectural fix, still underexplored, is fertility-aware positional encoding that normalizes the positional span of multi-token morpheme decompositions before they enter the attention stack, so that a 5-token Turkish word and its 1-token English equivalent occupy comparable positional footprints — without this, even adapter-based methods are treating a symptom rather than the structural cause of upper-layer overwriting.

The isolation critique is valid and measurable: in the original MAD-X framework, language adapters and task adapters are stacked sequentially (language adapter → task adapter → output), meaning task-specific transformations learned on the pivot are applied after language-specific re-projection, creating an implicit assumption that task knowledge is language-neutral — an assumption that breaks for tasks where morphological structure is task-relevant, such as dependency parsing or morphological tagging, where the task adapter trained on English encodes English-specific syntactic surface patterns that don't compose cleanly with Turkish subword representations routed through the language adapter. The principled solution is adapter fusion (Pfeiffer et al., 2021), which trains a learned attention mechanism over a set of pre-trained task adapters from multiple languages, allowing the low-resource target to dynamically weight contributions from pivot task adapters rather than inheriting them wholesale — this recovered 3–8 F1 on cross-lingual NER for Swahili and Yoruba by allowing partial task knowledge transfer without overwriting the language adapter's representational structure. A topologically distinct approach is invertible adapters (also in MAD-X), which apply bijective transformations that can be composed and inverted, so the language-specific projection can be "undone" at the task adapter boundary and "redone" afterward — this allows task adapters to operate in a more language-neutral space while still benefiting from language-specific surface normalization at input/output boundaries. The key design principle emerging from these results is that knowledge flow should be gated by representational compatibility: Üstün et al. (2022) in their work on language-family adapters showed that grouping typologically similar languages (by morphological complexity, fertility range, or WALS features) and sharing adapters within groups — while maintaining isolation across groups — achieved better task transfer than either full sharing or full isolation, because intra-group languages have sufficiently similar subword granularity that task knowledge composes without overwrite risk. The remaining open problem is that adapter topology is currently hand-designed based on linguistic priors; a fully learned routing mechanism that dynamically adjusts knowledge flow based on online measurement of representational compatibility between source and target at each layer would be more principled, but no system has successfully trained such routing end-to-end without collapsing to either full isolation or full sharing.

The honest answer from probing studies is that adapter fusion attention weights correlate more strongly with corpus-level distributional overlap than with linguistically meaningful structural compatibility — Pfeiffer et al. (2021) noted that fusion weights for target languages consistently up-weighted adapters from languages with similar pretraining data composition (domain, genre, formality) rather than languages with similar morphological typology, suggesting the fusion mechanism is tracking something closer to topic similarity than transfer-relevant structural affinity. Moosavi et al. (2022) probed fusion attention patterns directly and found that high fusion weights between a source adapter and target context predicted transfer success on surface tasks (POS tagging, NER boundary detection) but failed to predict transfer on structural tasks (dependency arc prediction, semantic role labeling), precisely where morphological fertility differences matter most — implying the signal the fusion learns is real but shallow. The mechanism likely works as follows: fusion attention operates on the hidden states produced by each candidate adapter, and those hidden states encode both task-relevant transformations and incidental corpus statistics from pretraining; for high-fertility target languages, the hidden states are structurally foreign enough that the fusion attention cannot find a geometrically close pivot adapter, so it defaults to weighting by surface similarity — the closest proxy available in representation space. This is empirically supported by the finding that fusion performance degrades monotonically with fertility differential between source adapters and target language (Üstün et al., 2022), and that replacing fusion attention with typology-informed hard routing (using WALS feature vectors to pre-select compatible adapters) matched or exceeded learned fusion on high-fertility targets while underperforming on low-fertility ones — exactly the pattern you'd expect if learned fusion is competent for similar-fertility languages but degenerates to noise for distant ones. The deeper epistemological problem is that without ground-truth labels for "linguistically meaningful compatibility," it's nearly impossible to distinguish a fusion mechanism that has learned genuine structural affinity from one that has learned a confounded proxy that happens to work on benchmark distributions — and current NLP benchmarks are sufficiently domain-homogeneous that the distinction may be invisible in aggregate metrics while mattering enormously for out-of-distribution transfer.

The most promising self-derived compatibility signal is representation space geometry: by measuring the mean cosine distance between token-level embeddings of a candidate source language and the target language in the shared embedding space — before any task fine-tuning — you get a proxy for how much representational restructuring the model would need to perform to align them, and this correlates with transfer success more reliably than WALS features for low-resource languages without external linguistic annotation (Eronen et al., 2023, showed this for zero-shot cross-lingual parsing across 30 languages including several with no WALS coverage). A more granular alternative is subword fertility profile similarity: computing the distribution of token-per-word ratios across a raw monolingual corpus for both source and target, then measuring KL divergence between these fertility distributions, gives a language-pair-level scalar that captures morphological complexity alignment without requiring any typological database — languages with similar fertility profiles tend to decompose meaning at similar granularities, making task adapter composition geometrically more compatible. Muller et al. (2021) demonstrated that overlap in the long tail of the shared vocabulary — specifically the fraction of tokens appearing fewer than 100 times in pretraining that are shared between two languages — predicts zero-shot transfer better than surface vocabulary overlap for morphologically rich languages, because rare shared tokens tend to be borrowed terms or proper nouns that anchor semantic alignment independently of morphological divergence. A fourth approach derives compatibility from centered kernel alignment (CKA) between layer-wise representations computed on a small parallel corpus (even 500–1000 sentences suffice): by profiling which layers show high CKA between source and target before fine-tuning, you can identify whether structural alignment exists at lower layers (favorable for task transfer) or only at upper layers (fragile, overwrite-prone), giving a richer compatibility signal than any single scalar. The key advantage of all four approaches is that they are computable from the model itself plus raw monolingual or minimal parallel data — but their limitation is that they measure current compatibility in the pretrained model, not potential compatibility after language-specific adaptation, meaning they may systematically underestimate transfer potential for languages that are structurally compatible but poorly represented in pretraining.

The curriculum idea is theoretically well-motivated and has partial empirical support: Chronopoulou et al. (2020) showed that continual multilingual pretraining ordered by language similarity — measured via character n-gram overlap as a proxy for structural proximity — reduced catastrophic forgetting and improved cross-lingual transfer compared to random ordering, with gains of 2–4 BLEU on low-resource translation, establishing that order matters in multilingual pretraining even when the final data mixture is identical. Extending this to fertility-aware curriculum design, the proposal would be to initialize with a core of low-fertility, high-resource languages (English, Chinese, Indonesian) to establish a stable geometric scaffold, then introduce languages in ascending order of fertility divergence from the current centroid of the shared space — measuring after each language addition whether CKA between existing languages and the new entrant falls below a disruption threshold before proceeding. The critical complication is that fertility divergence and embedding geometry can conflict as ordering signals: Arabic has moderate fertility but extreme script and morphological divergence from Latin-script languages, meaning a geometry-first curriculum would delay it heavily while a fertility-first curriculum would introduce it relatively early — and no existing work has systematically resolved which signal should dominate or how to combine them into a single curriculum ordering criterion. A dynamic rather than static curriculum offers a partial solution: Wang et al. (2020) in their work on multilingual neural machine translation used language competence scores — online measurements of per-language perplexity relative to a baseline — to up-sample languages the model was currently struggling with, effectively implementing a feedback-driven curriculum; adapting this to geometric disruption would mean measuring post-addition CKA degradation and triggering remedial rehearsal of previously stable languages when disruption exceeds threshold. The deeper problem is that geometric disruption during pretraining is not purely bad: some restructuring of the shared space is necessary for high-fertility languages to achieve adequate representation, and a curriculum that minimizes disruption too aggressively may produce a space that is geometrically stable but systematically biased toward the low-fertility languages that anchored it — the right objective is not minimum disruption but controlled disruption that expands the representable manifold without collapsing existing structure.

A disruption budget can be operationalized as a per-layer CKA degradation bound: before introducing a new language batch, compute baseline CKA between all existing language pairs at each layer; after each gradient update, measure CKA again and halt or rescale the update if degradation exceeds a threshold δ (e.g., 0.05 CKA units) in layers identified as carrying cross-lingual alignment signal — this converts an abstract geometric goal into a concrete per-step constraint that can be monitored online without requiring held-out parallel data beyond what's used for the CKA probe. The regularization mechanism that most naturally implements selective expansion rather than overwrite is elastic weight consolidation (EWC) adapted to the multilingual setting: compute Fisher information over parameters with respect to existing language performance, then penalize updates that move high-Fisher parameters — those critical to existing language representations — while leaving low-Fisher parameters free to be recruited for new language structure; Artetxe et al. (2020) demonstrated that EWC-style regularization during language addition to a pretrained model preserved existing language quality while still achieving competitive performance on newly added languages, with the key insight that low-resource language addition primarily requires recruiting unused parameter capacity rather than overwriting existing structure. A more targeted mechanism is gradient projection (Saha et al., 2021, in the continual learning literature): project incoming gradients from new-language batches onto the null space of the gradient subspace spanned by existing languages, ensuring new-language updates are orthogonal to directions that matter for existing representations — this is geometrically precise but computationally expensive, requiring maintenance of a gradient subspace basis that grows with each added language. The expansion-vs-overwrite distinction can be made explicit by monitoring intrinsic dimensionality of the shared representation space (using TwoNN or similar estimators) before and after each language addition: if intrinsic dimensionality increases, the manifold is genuinely expanding to accommodate new structure; if it stays constant while existing language CKA degrades, the budget is being spent on overwriting rather than expansion, triggering stronger EWC penalties or gradient projection. The unresolved tension is that gradient projection and EWC both treat existing language structure as equally worth preserving, but some existing structure encodes low-frequency surface patterns that should be overwritten by more general cross-lingual representations — a truly principled disruption budget would need to distinguish parameter subspaces encoding generalizable cross-lingual abstractions from those encoding language-specific surface accidents, a decomposition that no current method achieves reliably.
